title: Make it decide
hook: Teach your program to choose: do this if true, do that if not.

warmup.q: Yesterday's Mad Libs: what does `word = input("Noun? ")` do?
options: Shows Noun? and waits for you to type
Picks a random noun for you
Prints Noun? and carries on at once
warmup.explain: input() shows the question, then waits. Whatever you type is stored in the name on the left, as text.
Two slashes mean divide and drop the leftover. 7 // 2 is 3. The leftover is what % gives you: 7 % 2 is 1.
The f before the quote lets you put a name in curly brackets. Python swaps in the stored value.

why.heading: Real life is full of ifs
why.text: A call sheet says: if it rains, shoot in the garage. Every crew decision works like that. So far your programs did every line, every time. The word **if** lets a program choose: run these lines only when something is true.

why.heading: The shape of an if
why.text:
Here it is:

`if hours > 10:`
`    print("Overtime")`

The line with `if` ends with a **colon**. The colon means: the lines that belong to this if are coming next. The condition (`hours > 10`) is a yes or no question.

why.heading: Indentation: the 4 spaces
why.text: Lines that belong to the if are pushed in by **4 spaces** (tap the space bar 4 times). That push is called **indentation**. Python uses it to see what is inside the if. Forget it and you get `IndentationError: expected an indented block`. Forget the colon and you get `SyntaxError: expected ':'`. Both name the line. Fix it and run again.

why.heading: Comparisons give True or False
why.text:
To ask a question you compare:

`==` equal to
`!=` not equal to
`<` less than, `>` more than
`<=` less or equal, `>=` more or equal

The answer is always `True` or `False`. Careful: one `=` stores a value, two `==` ask if two things are equal.

why.heading: else: the other road
why.text: `else:` runs when the if was False. It sits at the left edge, lines up with the `if`, has its own colon, and its own indented lines. Exactly one road is taken: the if lines OR the else lines, never both.

watch.intro: Tap Run. The program asks itself a question and picks a road. Then change `hours` to 8 and run again.
watch.code:
hours = 12
print(f"Hours worked: {hours}")
if hours > 10:
    print("Overtime!")
else:
    print("Normal day")
print("Done")
explain: `hours > 10` is True for 12, so Python runs the indented line and skips the else part.
With 8 it is False, so Python skips the if lines and runs the else lines.
`print("Done")` is not pushed in, so it runs every time, whatever happened above.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: delete the colon at the end of line 3 (the `if` line) and run. You get `SyntaxError: expected ':'`. Put it back. Now delete the 4 spaces before `print("Overtime!")` and run. You get `IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 3`. Put the spaces back.

tasks.title: Bring water
tasks.task: It is 35 degrees. Under the `if` line, add one pushed-in line (4 spaces) that shows exactly: `Bring water`
hints: Replace the comment line with a print line. Keep the 4 spaces at the start.
The shape is: 4 spaces, then print("your text").

tasks.title: Overtime check
tasks.task:
Ask for the hours worked. If it is MORE than 10, show `Overtime`. Otherwise show `Normal day`. Example with 12:

`Hours worked? 12`
`Overtime`
tasks.starter:
hours = int(input("Hours worked? "))
# add your if and else here
hints: You need if, a condition, a colon, then a pushed-in print. Then else, a colon, a pushed-in print.
The condition is hours > 10. Exactly 10 hours is NOT overtime, so use > and not >=.

tasks.title: Fix the door code
tasks.task: This door code check has five small mistakes: a wrong `=`, two missing colons and two missing indents. Fix them. If you type `ICL` it shows `Welcome on set`. Anything else shows `Access denied`.
tasks.starter:
code = input("Crew code? ")
if code = "ICL"
print("Welcome on set")
else
print("Access denied")
hints: Fix the first error Python names, run again, repeat. One at a time.
To compare you need two equals: ==. Both if and else need a colon at the end. The two print lines need 4 spaces at the start.
if code == "ICL":  then a pushed-in print, then else:  then a pushed-in print.

tests.expect:
Crew code? ICL
Welcome on set

recap: `if condition:` runs the indented lines only when the condition is True.
The colon ends the if line. The 4 spaces show which lines belong to it.
`==` asks if equal. `!=` not equal. `<` `>` `<=` `>=` compare numbers.
`else:` runs when the if was False. One road or the other, never both.

words.meaning: The yes or no question after if.
The only two answers a condition can give.
The 4 spaces at the start of a line that show it belongs inside.
Two equals signs: asks if two things are equal. One = stores a value.
The road taken when the if was False.
